source.title: Junior School Curriculum Design — Social Studies, Grade 7
source.notes: Read in full via the Read tool (no pages param). First published 2022, Revised 2024. Backfilled retroactively — skills already shipped in web/src/skills/socialStudiesG7/ before this record was written. 5 strands: 1.0 Social Studies and Personal Development, 2.0 People and Relationships, 3.0 Community Service Learning, 4.0 Natural and Historic Built Environments, 5.0 Political Development and Governance (120 lessons total). Discrepancy noted: Appendix 2's assessment-methods table uses slightly different sub-strand names/numbering for strand 2.0 (e.g. '2.4 Socio-economic organization of selected communities in Africa up to 1900', '2.6 Human Diversity and Inclusion', '2.7 Peace and Non-Violent Conflict Resolution') than the main body text (2.4 Developments in medium of Trade, 2.5 Diversity and interpersonal relationships, 2.6 Peaceful Coexistence) — the main body (which carries the actual outcomes/experiences/PCIs) is treated as authoritative here, per the same precedent set for Grade 7 Mathematics' Appendix-vs-body discrepancy. Appendix 2 also names the specific communities for sub-strand 5.1 ('The Ogiek, the Zulu and the Asante') that the main body text only references generically as 'the selected African communities' — captured in that sub-strand's scopeNotes since it is the only place in the source that names them.

subStrands.name: 1.1 Self-Exploration
specificLearningOutcomes: explore personal abilities and interests for holistic development
develop personal values for a steady personality
manage emotions in day-to-day life
appreciate personal awareness in day-to-day life
keyInquiryQuestions: How can personal abilities and interests influence career choices?
learningExperiences: reflect and journal personal abilities and interests and share with a friend in class
brainstorm on how to use personal abilities and interests for holistic development and make presentations in class
share personal values/principles that help him or her pull through as a steady person
use print or digital resources to search for how to develop personal principles and share in class
search using digital or print media how to manage emotions (happiness, love, fear and anger) in day-to-day life
share previous experiences in groups how he/she dealt with emotions
watch relevant video clips or print media on effective management of emotions in day-to-day life
linkedLearningAreas: English/Kiswahili/KSL: speaking and listening skills used to brainstorm on personal abilities and interests for holistic development.

subStrands.name: 1.2 Entrepreneurial Opportunities in Social Studies
specificLearningOutcomes: identify entrepreneurial opportunities that closely match their personality
describe requirements for social entrepreneurial opportunities in the world of work
appreciate entrepreneurial opportunities in social studies
keyInquiryQuestions: What is entrepreneurship?
Which entrepreneurial opportunities exist in society?
learningExperiences: use digital or print media to search and classify entrepreneurial opportunities in social studies and make a presentation in class
create posters of common entrepreneurial opportunities in social studies and display in class
use digital or print media to find out the personality requirements for any five social studies entrepreneurial opportunities in day to day life and make presentations in class
draw charts showing alignment of personal talents or abilities with different entrepreneurial opportunities in the country
engage a relevant resource person to give a talk on entrepreneurial opportunities versus personality types
linkedLearningAreas: Pre-Technical Studies: charts aligning personal talents and abilities with available entrepreneurial opportunities.

subStrands.name: 2.1 Human Origin
specificLearningOutcomes: explore traditional stories of human origin from African communities
explain religious stories about the origin of humankind
illustrate common aspects found in traditional and religious stories of human origin
acknowledge religious and traditional stories of human origin
keyInquiryQuestions: How did human beings come to be?
learningExperiences: engage a resource person to discuss the traditional and religious stories on human origin from different communities
compare the different stories on human origin from their communities and share in class
write a collaborative essay on traditional and religious stories of human origin
record traditional stories about the origin of humankind in society
use relevant print or electronic media resources to research and present in class the traditional and religious stories about the origin of humankind
discuss ways of recording traditional stories about the origin of humankind in society
discuss the implications of the traditional and religious stories on human origin
linkedLearningAreas: Religious Education: creation stories.

subStrands.name: 2.2 Early Civilization
specificLearningOutcomes: explore factors that led to the growth of the selected ancient Kingdoms in Africa
locate the selected ancient Kingdoms on a map of Africa
assess the contribution of ancient Kingdoms to the modern world civilisation
appreciate the contribution of ancient kingdoms to the development of the modern world
keyInquiryQuestions: How has early African civilization influenced the world today?
learningExperiences: brainstorm on factors that led to the growth of ancient Egypt, Great Zimbabwe, and the Kingdom of Kongo
use appropriate digital or print media to find out the location of ancient Egypt, Great Zimbabwe, and the Kingdom of Kongo from the map of Africa
watch and critique audio-visual documentary on the contribution of Ancient Kingdoms to the modern world civilisation
write an essay on the contribution of ancient Kingdoms to the development of the modern world civilisation and present it in class
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts: architectural designs, dressing and artefacts.

subStrands.name: 2.3 Slavery and Servitude
specificLearningOutcomes: identify the various forms of slavery and servitude in traditional African society
explain factors which led to development of Indian ocean slave trade
sketch the geographical extent of the regions covered by Indian Ocean slave trade in Africa
desire to promote human dignity for a just and peaceful world
keyInquiryQuestions: Why has slavery and servitude existed for thousands of years?
learningExperiences: brainstorm on the meaning of slavery and servitude and share their findings in class
discuss various forms of slavery and servitude in traditional African society
use digital or print resource to find out the factors which led to development of Indian ocean slave trade
draw the geographical extent of the regions covered by the Indian Ocean Slave trade in Africa
debate on various social injustices committed to the Africans during Indian ocean slave trade in 15th century
develop slogans on ways of promoting human dignity for a just and peaceful world and share in class
linkedLearningAreas: English/Kiswahili/KSL: speaking skill used to brainstorm on forms of slavery and servitude.

subStrands.name: 2.4 Developments in Medium of Trade
specificLearningOutcomes: compare barter trade and the use of currency trade in Africa
trace the factors that led to introduction of money in Africa
deduce the impact of introduction of money in Africa
appreciate medium of trade for sustainability
keyInquiryQuestions: How has money transformed trade in Africa?
learningExperiences: brainstorm on what is barter trade
discuss the comparison between barter trade and use of currency in Africa
use digital/print media to find out factors that led to introduction of money in Africa
brainstorm on the impact of introduction of money in Africa
engage a resource person to give a talk on the impact of the introduction of money in Africa
role play barter trade and the use of currency trade in Africa and provide a critique
linkedLearningAreas: Pre-Technical Studies: impact of introduction of currency in Africa.

subStrands.name: 2.5 Diversity and Interpersonal Relationships
specificLearningOutcomes: identify factors that determine human diversity in the society
explain interpersonal skills that enhance healthy interactions in a multicultural society
classify the desirable and undesirable personality attributes
appreciate the importance of building healthy relationships in multicultural society
keyInquiryQuestions: How do varied personalities shape society?
Why is respect and appreciation of diversity crucial for social cohesion?
learningExperiences: brainstorm on what is human diversity
use digital or print materials to search for factors that determine human diversity
debate and classify desirable and undesirable personality attributes
role play in class the personality attributes that enhance self-awareness
outline personality attributes to enhance self-awareness
engage a resource person to discuss life skills that would promote healthy interactions in a multi-cultural society (effective communication, negotiation skills, assertiveness, empathy)
research using appropriate print, library resources or digital devices on the components of human identity in a multi-cultural society
role play the importance of building healthy relationships in a multicultural society
linkedLearningAreas: English/Kiswahili/KSL: brainstorm on desirable and undesirable personality attributes.

subStrands.name: 2.6 Peaceful Coexistence
specificLearningOutcomes: outline qualities of a peaceful person in the community
explore factors that promote peaceful co-existence
assess peaceful conflict resolution process in day-to-day life
value importance of peaceful coexistence in the community in day-to-day life
keyInquiryQuestions: How can we promote peace for mutual social well-being?
How can I manage stress and emotion to promote inner peace?
learningExperiences: brainstorm on qualities of a peaceful person in the community
write an essay on qualities of a peaceful person
use digital or print resources to find out peaceful conflict resolution process
engage a resource person to give a talk on factors that promote peaceful co-existence
role play peaceful conflict resolution process in day-to-day life
compose and recite peace poems on the importance of peaceful co-existence in the community in day-to-day life
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts and Sports: creative skills to compose and recite peace poems.

subStrands.name: 3.1 Community Service Learning Project
specificLearningOutcomes: explain the meaning of key terms used in community service learning (CSL) and CSL projects
describe the importance of CSL in the community
outline steps of a CSL project/activity
execute a class CSL project
desire to conduct CSL project in the community
keyInquiryQuestions: How can community service learning contribute to community development?
learningExperiences: brainstorm on the meaning of the terms community, community services, community service learning (CSL), project (activities outside class), problem (gaps or opportunities), solution (remedy), plan of activity, implementation, written report of a project

discuss the steps involved in carrying out a CSL project: identification and verification of a problem/gap/opportunity, planning to solve an identified problem, designing solution(s) to the problem, implementing the solution/filling the gap, reflecting and reporting on the project/activity done
identify and brainstorm on problems/gaps in their context/community
discuss, verify and adopt one problem for the class/groups project
propose and plan way(s) of solving the problem
implement the solution of the problem in the community
write and report on the accomplished project
discuss CSL benefits for self and the community
linkedLearningAreas: All subjects — they provide PCIs and undertake CSL activities.
scopeNotes: include: 6-step milestone approach — problem identification, designing a solution, planning for the project, implementation, showcasing/exhibition and report writing, reflection (see Appendix 1: Guidelines for Integrating Community Service Learning Project).

strands.name: 4.0 Natural and Historic Built Environments in Africa

subStrands.name: 4.1 Historical Information
specificLearningOutcomes: identify various sources of historical information in the society
distinguish between primary and secondary sources of historical information
explore how various sources of historical information have been preserved over the years
appreciate the significance of various sources of historical information in providing evidence of past human accounts
keyInquiryQuestions: How significant are sources of historical information in understanding past human accounts?
learningExperiences: use appropriate print media or digital resources to identify sources of historical information in the society and share in class
design posters on primary and secondary sources of historical information in the society and display in class
discuss ways of preserving sources of historical information
debate on the significance of various sources of historical information in providing evidence of past human accounts
engage a relevant resource person on historical information
linkedLearningAreas: English/Kiswahili/KSL: listening and speaking skills discussing sources of historical information.
Creative Arts: designing posters on primary and secondary sources of historical information.
pertinentContemporaryIssues: Self-awareness — career exploration in agro/animal husbandry

subStrands.name: 4.2 Historical Development of Agriculture
specificLearningOutcomes: locate areas where early agriculture was practised in selected geographical regions in Africa
explore crops grown and animals kept in selected regions during early agriculture
illustrate methods of irrigation used in ancient Egypt
assess the contribution of the Nile valley agriculture to world civilization
explore possible careers in Agriculture
value the importance of domestication of plants and animals in Africa
keyInquiryQuestions: Why did people start practising agriculture in Africa?
How did Agriculture begin in Africa?
learningExperiences: use appropriate digital devices and other sources to draw the map of Africa and show areas where early agriculture was practised in selected geographical regions (Rift Valley of Eastern Africa, Egypt and Nubia)

carry out research in groups on animals kept and types of crops which were grown during early agriculture in Egypt, Nubia and in the Rift Valley of the Eastern African region and report the findings to the class
view video clips or photographs on methods of irrigation used in ancient Egypt
draw diagrams showing methods of irrigation which were used in ancient Egypt
discuss the contribution of the Nile valley agriculture to world civilisation
collect/download pictures and photographs of different animals kept, crops grown in subsistence farming and methods of irrigation used during early agriculture in Egypt
discuss different careers associated with agro farming and animal husbandry
linkedLearningAreas: Agriculture and Nutrition: knowledge of animal husbandry researching animals kept and crops grown.
Creative Arts: creative skills drawing diagrams showing methods of irrigation.

subStrands.name: 4.3 Maps and Map Work
specificLearningOutcomes: describe the position, shape and size of Africa
locate places and features using latitudes and longitudes on a map
calculate the time of different places in the world
appreciate the location of key features in the continent
keyInquiryQuestions: How are maps used?
Why is time different in various locations?
learningExperiences: brainstorm on the position, shape and size of Africa and share in class
buzz on the countries that make up Africa and display in class
draw an outline map of Africa creatively and indicate the countries that make up Africa and display in class
use relevant print media or digital devices to establish the position and location of places and features on a map
calculate time of different places using longitudes
research on the three types of maps used in Social Studies and make summary notes (Topographical maps, Sketch maps and Atlas Maps)
discuss the three types of maps in Social Studies
discuss and appreciate positive features that are associated with Africa
linkedLearningAreas: Mathematics: calculation skills using longitudes to calculate time of different places in the world.

subStrands.name: 4.4 Earth and the Solar System
specificLearningOutcomes: describe the origin of the earth
explore the size, shape and position of the earth in the solar system
examine the effects of rotation and revolution of the earth on human activities
illustrate the internal structure of the earth in the solar system
appreciate the effects of rotation and revolution of the earth on human activities
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is it important to understand the solar system?
learningExperiences: share stories on the origin of the earth from their communities
use relevant print or digital resources to find out about the theories explaining the origin of the earth (the passing star theory and the nebula cloud theory)
brainstorm on the size, shape and position of the earth in the solar system
carry out library research on effects of rotation and revolution of the earth on human activities
draw the solar system and indicate the position of the earth as the home of humankind
draw the internal structure of the earth and display in class (core, mantle and crust)
develop communication messages on the effects of rotation and revolution of the earth on human activities
linkedLearningAreas: Integrated Science: computing skills used to research theories explaining the origin of the earth.

subStrands.name: 4.5 Weather
specificLearningOutcomes: describe the elements of weather in the environment
construct selected instruments for measuring elements of weather
examine the significance of weather to human environment
respond appropriately to different weather conditions in the environment
keyInquiryQuestions: Why are elements of weather in the environment important?
How can we predict change in weather conditions?
learningExperiences: use relevant print or digital resources to research the elements of weather in the environment and write a report
record and calculate weather conditions in the local environment (temperature, rainfall)
discuss the factors considered when constructing and siting a weather station in the school compound
use locally available materials to construct selected instruments for measuring elements of weather (a rain gauge/wind vane/windsock) and peer assess
brainstorm on the significance of weather to the human environment and how to appropriately change to varied weather conditions
discuss effects of weather on road safety
invite a resource person from a meteorological station to discuss possible careers related to climate
linkedLearningAreas: Mathematics: recording and calculating weather conditions in the local environment.

subStrands.name: 4.6 Fieldwork
specificLearningOutcomes: examine methods of data collection used in field work
use analysis methods to process data from the field work
explore solutions to challenges in carrying out field work
value field work in investigating phenomena
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is field work important in social studies?
How should we conduct field work?
learningExperiences: use digital devices to search for methods of data collection (observation, questionnaire, interview and focus group discussion)
engage an NTSA officer or any other relevant road officer to discuss current road safety data in the locality
use mean, median and mode to analyse road safety data from the locality and present in class
brainstorm on challenges likely to be encountered during field work and possible solutions
carry out fieldwork to investigate phenomena in the immediate environment
linkedLearningAreas: English/Kiswahili/KSL: listening and speaking skills discussing challenges likely to be encountered during field work.
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Non-formal activities row (Appendix 2) explicitly suggests initiating a road-safety club that continually offers road-safety awareness to peers and community — beyond the bare fieldwork outcome text, this signals a sustained/ongoing application, not a one-off exercise.

subStrands.name: 5.1 Political Development in Africa
specificLearningOutcomes: explore roles of European groups in the 'Scramble for and Partition' of Africa
examine the terms of the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885 on the partitioning of Africa
locate the regions partitioned by the European groups that came to Africa
acknowledge the political organisation of the selected African communities up to 1900
keyInquiryQuestions: How did developments in Europe influence the scramble and partition of Africa?
learningExperiences: discuss the various European groups that came to Africa and share
brainstorm on the terms 'Scramble for and Partition' of Africa and make presentations
match the countries in Africa with their colonial masters

draw the map of Africa and indicate the areas taken up by the different European countries (Belgium, Britain, Germany, Italy, Spain and Portugal) during the partition of Africa and display them in class
using posters display in class the terms of the Berlin conference of 1884-1885 on the partitioning of Africa
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts: drawing the map of Africa and indicating areas taken up by European countries.
scopeNotes: include: the specific 'selected African communities' referenced by the political-organisation outcome are named only in Appendix 2's non-formal-activities table as The Ogiek, the Zulu and the Asante — the main body's outcome/experience text does not itself enumerate them.

subStrands.name: 5.2 The Constitution of Kenya
specificLearningOutcomes: discuss the importance of the Constitution of Kenya
analyse ways of upholding and protecting the Constitution of Kenya for social cohesion
apply the national values in day-to-day life as provided in the Constitution of Kenya
uphold and protect the Constitution of Kenya to promote ethical and responsible citizenship
keyInquiryQuestions: Why should a country have a constitution?
Why should we uphold and protect the Constitution?
learningExperiences: use print or digital devices to conduct online research and write an essay on the importance of the Constitution and share in class
watch a video on the promulgation of the Constitution of Kenya and discuss in class
design a sample constitution for the class and display in class
write simple slogans or statements on any eight of the national values as provided in the Constitution of Kenya and present in class
discuss ways of upholding and protecting the Constitution of Kenya
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts and Sports: composing songs, writing slogans and making presentations.

subStrands.name: 5.3 Human Rights
specificLearningOutcomes: classify human rights as stipulated in the human rights instruments
explore characteristics of human rights in the society
explain the concept of equity and non-discrimination in fostering solidarity
take action to promote equity and non-discrimination for social justice
value human rights for promotion of human dignity
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is it important to know our rights?
How can we promote equity and non-discrimination in society?
How can we promote respect for human rights in our community?
learningExperiences: create posters on the classification of human rights and display them in school
use a tree diagram to indicate characteristics of human rights and display in class
brainstorm on issues of equity and non-discrimination
develop posters on equity and non-discrimination and display them in school
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts: graphic designs used to develop posters on equity and non-discrimination.

subStrands.name: 5.4 African Diasporas
specificLearningOutcomes: explore the factors that contributed to the presence of African diasporas across the world
locate countries inhabited by African diasporas by 1960 on a world map
assess the role of the diasporas in the political development in Africa
acknowledge the African diasporas and promotion of African unity in society today
keyInquiryQuestions: How can we promote collaboration between continental Africans and African Diasporas?
How can we promote African Unity in society today?
learningExperiences: with the aid of print or internet resources, discuss the concept of African diasporas
use library resources to research on the factors that contributed to the presence of African diasporas across the world and share the findings in class
use print or digital resources to locate on the world map countries inhabited by African diasporas by 1960 (USA, Brazil and France) and present in class
watch a video or YouTube on the role of the diasporas in the political development in Africa
debate on the role of the diasporas in the political development in Africa
develop simple slogans on the African diasporas and promotion of African unity in society today
linkedLearningAreas: Computer/ICT: computer skills watching video on the role of diasporas in political development.

subStrands.name: 5.5 Citizenship
specificLearningOutcomes: explain why there is interconnectedness and interdependence among countries in the world today
examine effects of globalisation at national and global levels
describe qualities of a global citizen in the modern society
create awareness on the effects of globalisation at national and global levels
contribute to the international community while maintaining loyalty to own country
keyInquiryQuestions: How do countries connect and depend on each other in the world today?
Which are the common concerns in the world today?
learningExperiences: discuss the interconnectedness and interdependence among countries in the world today
read news articles in newspapers or use appropriate media to find out aspects that promote globalisation in the community and share the information in class
debate on positive and negative effects of globalisation at local and national levels
brainstorm on the qualities of a global citizen in the modern society
use print or digital resources to research for qualities of a global citizen and write them down
draw a sketch of a palm and indicate qualities of a global citizen
sing the National, East Africa and African Union anthems
linkedLearningAreas: Computer/ICT: computer skills researching qualities of a global citizen using print or digital resources.
